title: Mega Man
subtitle: the whole franchise, by sub-series, in release order
blurb: 95 games — every one with Mega Man on the box, from the 1987 NES original to the offline X Dive, with Dual Override still to come. 59 carry a verified story length, about 307 hours between them.
notes: One source, and it chose the scope.

This is “the mega man compendium” on Backloggd — one person's list, described by its own author as “every mega man game ever sorted by release date”. That is why the licensed Chinese PC releases and a decade of Japanese feature-phone toys are here: the compendium counts them, so this counts them. Nothing has been dropped, and one game has been added: Mega Man: Dual Override, the next Classic game, dated 2027.
The sections are not the source's.

The compendium has none — it is one flat grid of 94, sorted by release date. The sections here read each title's own sub-series off its name, and the order inside every one of them is still the compendium's: release date, oldest first. Read a section top to bottom and you are reading that branch exactly as the compendium has it. Dual Override, the one addition, comes last in Classic.
36 of the 95 have no length, and none has been invented.

Hours are HowLongToBeat main-story figures, and only where a record verifies by name and by release year. 20 rows have no such record at all — the arcade cabinets, the Japanese feature-phone games, the licensed Chinese PC releases — and a plausible-looking guess for any of them would go straight into your finish date. 15 more are the paired versions below. All 35 say which they are and count as an hour apiece: a floor, not a claim. The last is Dual Override, which is not out yet and weighs nothing until it is.
Paired versions are separate rows, and deliberately unweighted.

Battle Network 3 through 6 and all three Star Force games shipped in two or three versions apiece, and the compendium lists every one. So does this. But HowLongToBeat times the numbered game rather than each version — there is one Battle Network 3 record, not a Blue and a White — and putting that figure on both rows would bill you twice for a game you play once. Playing one of a pair is the normal thing to do; tick the one you played.
What “release order” means for a 95-game list.

Everything is dated from its own Backloggd page except Dual Override, which carries the year Capcom announced. Where two games share a year the compendium's order is kept as it stands — the source sorted them, not this file. Three of its entries are called nothing but Mega Man: the 1987 NES game, an American-built DOS game from 1990, and a North American Game Gear release from 1995. The later two carry their platform in brackets here so they can be told apart; that is the only place a title has been changed.

Contents and order from “the mega man compendium” by ade on Backloggd; years from each game's Backloggd page, Dual Override's from Wikipedia; story hours from HowLongToBeat, verified by name and release year.

sections.title: Classic
sections.intro: The blue one, the numbered line, and everything that plays like it: the NES six, the five Game Boy entries, the 16-bit and 32-bit sequels, the two American-built DOS games, the remakes, and the eight-bit throwbacks that restarted the count in 2008.

items.note: NES. The first one: eight Robot Masters, a stage you pick, and the rule that beating one hands you its weapon.
NES. The one that fixed the formula and sold; still the series' front door.
NES. Adds the slide and Rush, the dog who turns into whatever you need to cross a gap.
DOS. Not a port — an American-built PC game with its own Robot Masters, licensed out and made outside Capcom.
Game Boy. The handheld line starts, drawing its bosses from the first two NES games.
NES. Introduces the chargeable Buster, which the series never takes back.
Game Boy. The second handheld entry, and the only one made by a different studio from the rest of the Game Boy line.
Game Boy. The handheld line back on its usual team, building from NES 3 and 4.
NES. Beat the bird joins the support cast.

items.t: Mega Man 3: The Robots are Revolting
items.note: DOS. The second and last of the American-built PC pair, and unrelated to the NES Mega Man 3.
Game Boy. Draws on NES 4 and 5, and adds a shop between stages.
NES. The last NES entry; Rush becomes armour you wear instead of a vehicle you ride.
Game Boy. The handheld line's finale, and the only one whose bosses are all original — the Stardroids.
Mega Drive. 16-bit remakes of the first three NES games plus a short original chapter; a cartridge in Japan and Europe, a Sega Channel download in North America.
SNES. The 16-bit Classic entry, with bigger sprites and a hub you shop in.
Game Gear. A handheld remix assembled from NES 4 and 5, released only in North America.
PlayStation and Saturn. The first with animated cutscenes and voice acting.
Super Famicom, later Game Boy Advance. Two playable characters who move very differently, built on Mega Man 8's engine.

items.t: Rockman & Forte: Mirai kara no Chousensha
items.note: WonderSwan, Japan only. A different game from Mega Man & Bass, despite sharing its Japanese name.
PSP. A remake of the 1987 original in a rounded style, with the Robot Masters playable and a stage editor.
Downloadable. A deliberate return to NES limits: eight-bit art, no slide, no charge shot.
Downloadable. The eight-bit follow-up, with an easy mode and extra playable characters.
The modern Classic entry: hand-drawn 2.5D art, and a gear system that will slow time or strengthen your shots at a price.
Not out yet — dated 2027, and the bar stays empty until HowLongToBeat has hours for it. The twelfth main Classic game and the first since 11, with Proto Man playable alongside Mega Man.

sections.title: X
sections.intro: The 1993 spin-off that gave the formula a dash, a wall climb and hidden armour upgrades, plus its handheld condensations, its RPG, its 3D detour and the remake.

items.note: SNES. The spin-off that adds a dash, a wall climb and armour upgrades hidden in the stages.
SNES. Uses a cartridge chip for wireframe effects, and adds an air dash.
SNES. Zero becomes playable in a limited way, and the ride armours branch out.
PlayStation and Saturn. Zero becomes a full second campaign with his own moveset.
Windows, China only. A licensed educational release wearing the X cast · HowLongToBeat has no story time for it
Game Boy Color. A handheld condensation of stages from X and X2.
PlayStation. Written as the line's ending, with Zero playable throughout.
Game Boy Color. The handheld follow-up, with X and Zero as separate campaigns.
PlayStation. Made quickly after X5, and the most contested entry in the line.
PlayStation 2. The move into 3D, and the debut of a third playable character.
GameCube and PS2. A turn-based RPG spin-off with a party to build.
PlayStation 2. Back to sidescrolling, with a mid-stage character swap.
PSP. A remake of the first X with reworked stages and a second campaign for Vile.
The one-purchase offline build of a live-service X action game, made after its servers closed.

items.note: GBA. The reboot into a networked world: real-time battles on a grid, fought with a deck of Battle Chips.
GBA. Doubles down on chip customisation and adds Style Changes.

sections.title: Everything else with Mega Man on the box
sections.intro: The Classic universe's odd jobs, which the compendium counts and most franchise summaries do not: two arcade boss-rush cabinets, a board game, football, a kart racer, an animated adventure, licensed Chinese PC releases, a decade of Japanese feature-phone toys, and the one crossover Capcom adopted from its own fans.
